title: Nehemiah Returns to Find Things Slipping
overview: After time away at the Persian court, Nehemiah comes back to Jerusalem and forcefully reverses a series of lapses in temple care, Sabbath rest and marriage practices.

parts.label: A law about outsiders (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: A public reading of the law turned up an old rule, found in Deuteronomy 23, barring Ammonites and Moabites from Israel's worshipping community because their ancestors refused Israel food and water and hired Balaam to curse them. The people then separated those of foreign descent, though scholars are unsure how widely this was applied, and the book of Ruth honors a Moabite woman as King David's ancestor.

parts.label: Tobiah evicted (vv. 4-9)
parts.note: Eliashib, the priest in charge of the temple storerooms, had close ties to Tobiah, an Ammonite official who had opposed Nehemiah's rebuilding, and gave him a large room inside the temple. When Nehemiah returned from serving the Persian king, he threw Tobiah's belongings out, had the rooms ritually cleansed, and put the sacred supplies back.

parts.label: Temple workers unpaid (vv. 10-14)
parts.note: The tithes, a tenth of the harvest meant to support the Levites and temple singers, were not reaching them, so they had gone home to farm and the temple was neglected. Nehemiah confronted the officials, called the workers back, put trusted people in charge of handing out supplies, and asked God to remember what he had done.

parts.label: Gates shut on the Sabbath (vv. 15-22)
parts.note: People were pressing grapes, hauling goods and buying fish from traders from Tyre, a coastal city to the north, on the Sabbath. Nehemiah linked this to the disasters that had once fallen on Jerusalem, shut the city gates for the day, and threatened to arrest merchants who camped outside the walls.

parts.label: Marriages and a harsh response (vv. 23-29)
parts.note: Some men of Judah had married women from Ashdod, Ammon and Moab, and half their children could not speak Judah's language, which Nehemiah saw as a threat to the community's faith and identity, pointing to how foreign wives had led King Solomon astray. He cursed and beat some of the men, pulled out their hair, made them swear an oath, and drove out the high priest's grandson, who had married into the family of his enemy Sanballat.

parts.label: Final ordering (vv. 30-31)
parts.note: Nehemiah reorganized the priests and Levites and arranged regular supplies of wood for the altar fire and of firstfruits, the first part of each harvest given to God. The book ends with him once more asking God to remember him for good.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Nehemiah's forceful separation from foreigners should be read as a model of faithful zeal for that moment or as a harsh, limited response that other biblical books like Ruth and Jonah seem to push against.
think: When a group feels its identity slipping away, where is the line between protecting what matters and shutting people out?
